1. Why is it called a “neuron”?

blocks.html: The idea comes from biology — from the brain. A brain cell is called a neuron (also: neural cell, neural processing unit). Deep learning borrows the name and a very rough version of how it works.

2. Many neurons, working
together

blocks.html: One neuron does not do all this. Your brain has about 10¹¹ = 100 billion neurons in a huge, massively parallel network.

blocks.html: Two big ideas from the brain:
blocks.text: Two big ideas from the brain:

blocks.html:
1. Division of work. Each neuron has its own job. In the lecture’s cartoon, one neuron fires “if the text is funny”, one “if the visual is funny”, one “if the speech style is funny”, and a top neuron fires “if at least 2 of these 3 fired”.
  2. Hierarchy (layers). In the visual cortex, information flows from the retina through layers V1, V2, … up to AIT. Lower layers find simple things; higher layers find complex things.

3. The McCulloch–Pitts (MP)
neuron (1943)

blocks.html: Warren McCulloch (a neuroscientist) and Walter Pitts (a logician) proposed the first, very simple, computational model of a neuron in 1943.
blocks.text:
Warren McCulloch (a neuroscientist) and Walter Pitts (a logician) proposed the first, very
simple, computational model of a neuron in 1943 .

blocks.alt: MP neuron: inputs go into g which adds them, then f compares with threshold theta
blocks.caption:
Two steps: g adds the inputs, f compares the sum with the threshold
θ.

blocks.html: The rules:
blocks.text: The rules:

blocks.html:
• Inputs x₁, x₂, …, xₙ are only 0 or 1 (Boolean).
  • Output y is also only 0 or 1.
  • Each input is either excitatory (normal) or inhibitory (a “veto” input).
blocks.text: Inputs x₁, x₂, …, xₙ are only 0 or 1 (Boolean). Output y is also only 0 or 1 . Each input is either excitatory (normal) or inhibitory (a “veto” input).

blocks.text: g(x) = x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ

blocks.html: Step 2 — f makes the decision:
blocks.text: Step 2 — f makes the decision:

blocks.html:
• y = 1 if g(x) ≥ θ
  • y = 0 if g(x) < θ
blocks.text: y = 1 if g(x) ≥ θ y = 0 if g(x) < θ

blocks.html: θ (theta) is called the thresholding parameter. This whole idea is called thresholding logic.

5. The
picture: one MP neuron draws one straight line

blocks.html: With 2 inputs there are only 4 possible points: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). The MP neuron fires when x₁ + x₂ ≥ θ. The boundary x₁ + x₂ = θ is a straight line.

sections.title: The Perceptron, Weights, Bias and Errors

blocks.html: Start here The MP neuron treats every input the same and needs a human to choose θ. In real life some reasons matter more than others. The perceptron gives each input its own weight, accepts real numbers, and — most importantly — can learn its weights from data.

Start here The MP neuron treats every input the same
and needs a human to choose θ. In real life some reasons matter more

can learn its weights from data.
1. Who made it?

blocks.html:
• Frank Rosenblatt, an American psychologist, proposed the perceptron in 1958.
  • Minsky and Papert (1969) refined and carefully analysed it. Their version is the “perceptron” used in this course.
blocks.text:

proposed the perceptron in 1958 . Minsky and Papert (1969) refined and carefully

blocks.text: 3. Why weights? Why “bias”?

blocks.html: Lecture example — will I like this movie? Inputs (0 or 1): x₁ = isActorDamon, x₂ = isGenreThriller, x₃ = isDirectorNolan. From past viewing we know Nolan movies are almost always liked. So we give w₃ a big weight. Even if the actor is not Matt Damon and it is not a thriller, w₃ alone can push the sum over the threshold.

sections.title: Perceptron Learning Algorithm and Its Proof of Convergence

blocks.html: Start here We don’t want to guess weights by hand. We want the perceptron to look at examples and fix itself whenever it makes a mistake. The Perceptron Learning Algorithm (PLA) does exactly that, using a simple rule: add the point if you wrongly said 0, subtract it if you wrongly said 1.
blocks.text:
Start here We don’t want to guess weights by hand.
We want the perceptron to look at examples and fix
itself whenever it makes a mistake. The Perceptron Learning
Algorithm (PLA) does exactly that, using a simple rule: add the
point if you wrongly said 0, subtract it if you wrongly said
1.

1. The perceptron as a
binary classifier

blocks.html: Lecture example — movie data We have m movies. For each movie we know whether the user liked it (1) or not (0). Each movie is described by n features, some 0/1 and some real: x₁ = isActorDamon, x₂ = isGenreThriller, x₃ = isDirectorNolan, x₄ = imdbRating (scaled 0–1), …, xₙ = criticsRating (scaled 0–1). We assume the data is linearly separable and want the perceptron to find the separating plane, i.e. find w₀, w₁, …, wₙ.
blocks.text:

blocks.html:
1. Start with the given w. Take the points in the given order.

  4. Count updates. “Converged” = one full pass with no update.
  5. Angle questions: cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖).

The story in 6 lines

blocks.html:
1. Biological neuron: dendrite (receives) → soma (processes) → axon (sends) → synapse (connects). The brain has ~10¹¹ neurons, works in parallel, and is organised in layers (simple → complex).
  2. MP neuron (1943): inputs 0/1, add them, output 1 if sum ≥ θ. Any inhibitory input = 1 → output 0.
  3. Perceptron (Rosenblatt 1958, refined by Minsky–Papert 1969): weights + real inputs + learnable bias. y = 1 if Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ wᵢxᵢ ≥ 0, with x₀ = 1, w₀ = −θ.
  4. PLA: wrong on a positive point → w = w + x; wrong on a negative point → w = w − x. Converges if the data is linearly separable.
  5. XOR is not linearly separable → one perceptron can’t do it.
  6. MLP: 1 hidden layer of 2ⁿ perceptrons + 1 output perceptron can represent any Boolean function of n inputs.

1. PLA: w = [0, 1, −1], negative point (2, 1). New w?
x = [1, 2, 1]; wᵀx = 0 + 2 − 1 = 1 ≥ 0 → wrong. w − x = [−1, −1, −2].

1. Why can’t one perceptron learn XOR?
Rows (0,1) and (1,0) force w₁ + w₂ ≥ −2w₀ > −w₀, but row (1,1) needs w₁ + w₂ < −w₀. Contradiction — XOR is not linearly separable.
